column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 47: “No human being fills a vessel worse than his stomach”

column2: From al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “No human being fills a vessel worse than a stomach.

A few mouthfuls are enough for the son of Ādam to keep his back upright. If he must [eat more], then a third for his food, a third for his drink and a third for his breath.” Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah reported it, and al-Tirmidhī said: A good (ḥasan) hadith.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded this hadith from the hadith of Yaḥyā ibn Jābir al-Ṭāʾī, from al-Miqdām.

Al-Nasāʾī recorded it by this route and by another, in the narration of Ṣāliḥ ibn Yaḥyā ibn al-Miqdām from his grandfather; Ibn Mājah recorded it from him by another route; and it has other routes as well.
This hadith has also been narrated together with what occasioned it. Abū al-Qāsim al-Baghawī narrated in his Muʿjam, from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Muraqqaʿ, who said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Khaybar when it was green with fruit. The people fell upon the fruit and were struck down with fever, and they complained of it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Fever is the forerunner of death and Allah's prison on earth, and it is a piece of the Fire.

When it seizes you, cool water in old waterskins and pour it over yourselves between the two prayers” — meaning Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. He said: They did that, and it left them. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Allah has not created a vessel worse, when it is filled, than a stomach. If it must be, then make a third for food, a third for drink and a third for air.”
This hadith is a comprehensive foundation for all the principles of medicine.

It is narrated that when the physician Ibn Abī Māsawayh read this hadith in the book of Abū Khaythamah, he said: If people put these words into practice, they would be safe from diseases and ailments, and the hospitals and the druggists' shops would stand idle. He said this only

because the root of every illness is surfeit (tukhamah) — as someone said: The root of every illness is indigestion (baradah). This has been narrated as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), but its attribution to him is not authentic.
Al-Ḥārith ibn Kaladah, the physician of the Arabs, said: Abstinence is the chief of remedies, and gluttony the chief of diseases. Some narrated this as marfūʿ, and that is not authentic either.
Al-Ḥārith also said: What has killed creation (al-bariyyah) and destroyed the beasts of the wilderness (al-barriyyah) is putting food on top of food before it has been digested.
Someone else said: If the people of the graves were asked what had brought on their deaths, they would say: Surfeit.
These, then, are some of the benefits of eating little and not filling oneself with food, as regards the soundness and health of the body.

As for its benefits for the heart and its soundness, eating little brings tenderness of heart, strength of understanding, humility of the self, and weakness of passion and anger, while eating much brings the opposite.
Al-Ḥasan said: Son of Ādam, eat in a third of your stomach, drink in a third, and leave a third of your stomach to breathe, so that you may reflect.

Al-Marrūdhī said: Abū ʿAbdillāh — meaning Aḥmad — began to speak of hunger and poverty as a great matter. I said to him: Is a man rewarded for giving up his appetites? He said: How could he not be rewarded, when Ibn ʿUmar says: I have not eaten my fill for four months?
I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh: Does a man find tenderness in his heart while he eats his fill?
He said: I do not think so.
Al-Marrūdhī narrated this saying of Ibn ʿUmar from Abū ʿAbdillāh by several routes. With his chain, he narrated from Ibn Sīrīn, who said: A man said to Ibn ʿUmar: Shall I bring you some jawārish?
He said: What is that?

He said: Something that digests your food after you have eaten. He said: I have not eaten my fill for four months, and not because I cannot; but I have known people who were hungry more often than they were full.
With his chain, from Nāfiʿ, who said: A man brought some jawārish to Ibn ʿUmar, and he said: What is this?
He said: Jawārish — something that helps food to digest. He said: What would I do with it?
A whole month passes over me in which I do not eat my fill of food.

With his chain, from a man who said: I said to Ibn ʿUmar: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, your chewing has grown weak and you have grown old, and those who sit with you do not recognise your due or your standing. If only you would tell your family to prepare something for you, to coax you with when you go back to them.

He said: Woe to you! By Allah, I have not eaten my fill even once for eleven years, nor twelve years, nor thirteen years, nor fourteen years. How could I, when all that is left of me is like a donkey's thirst [a brief span]?
With his chain, from ʿAmr ibn al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī: He used to stop well short of being full, for fear of growing insolent.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated in his book al-Jūʿ (“Hunger”), with his chain, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: I have not eaten my fill since I became Muslim.

He narrated with his chain from Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ, who said: Whoever eats little understands, makes others understand, and becomes pure and tender. Eating much weighs a person down from much of what he wants to do.

From Abū ʿUbaydah al-Khawwāṣ, who said: Your ruin lies in your being full, and your good fortune in your hunger. When you are full, you grow heavy and fall asleep, and the enemy gets a hold on you and sits on top of you; but when you keep yourself hungry, you lie in wait for the enemy.
From ʿAmr ibn Qays, who said: Beware of a full belly, for it hardens the heart.
From Salamah ibn Saʿīd, who said: A man used to be reproached for a full belly just as he would be reproached for a sin he had committed.
From one of the scholars, who said: If you are big-bellied, count yourself as crippled until your belly is lean.
From Ibn al-Aʿrābī, who said: The Arabs used to say: No man ever spent the night with a full belly and saw his resolve through.
From Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, who said: When you want to accomplish some need of this world or the Hereafter, do not eat until you have accomplished it, for eating alters the mind.
From Mālik ibn Dīnār, who said: It is not fitting for the believer that his stomach be his greatest concern, or that his appetite be what overpowers him.
He said: Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me: Al-Ḥasan, or someone else, said: The trial of your father Ādam (peace be upon him) was a meal, and it is your trial until the Day of Resurrection.
He said: It used to be said: Whoever masters his stomach masters all righteous deeds. And it used to be said: Wisdom does not dwell in a full stomach.
From ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād, who said: It used to be said: Eating little helps one to hasten towards good deeds.
From Qutham the worshipper, who said: It used to be said: No one ever ate little without his heart growing tender and his eyes moist.

From ʿAbdullāh ibn Marzūq, who said: We have seen nothing to match constant hunger against insolence. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿUmarī the ascetic said to him: And what, in your view, is keeping it constant?
He said: Keeping it constant is never eating your fill.
He said: And how can anyone in this world manage that?
He said: How easy that is, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, for those whom He has taken as His friends and granted success in obeying Him! Eating only short of one's fill — that is constant hunger.

Similar to this is what al-Ḥasan said when he offered food to one of his companions and the man said to him: I have eaten until I cannot eat any more. Al-Ḥasan said: Glory be to Allah! Does a Muslim eat until he cannot eat any more?!
He also narrated with his chain from Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, who said: It used to be said: Whoever would like his heart to be illuminated, let him eat little.
From ʿUthmān ibn Zāʾidah, who said: Sufyān al-Thawrī wrote to me: If you want your body to be healthy and your sleep to be little, eat less.
From Ibn al-Sammāk, who said: A man was alone with his brother and said: My brother, we are too insignificant to Allah for Him to make us go hungry; it is only His friends that He makes go hungry.
From ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Faraj, who said: I said to Abū Saʿīd al-Tamīmī: Does the one who fears [Allah] eat his fill?
He said: No. I said: Does the one who yearns [for Him] eat his fill? He said: No.

It is related of Riyāḥ al-Qaysī that food was set before him and he ate some of it. He was told: Have more, for I do not think you have eaten your fill. He let out a cry and said: How can I eat my fill in the days of this world, when the tree of Zaqqūm, the food of the sinner, lies before me?
The man took the food away from in front of him and said: You are in one state, and we are in another.
Al-Marrūdhī said: A man said to me: How is that man of ease?
— meaning Aḥmad. I said to him: And how is he a man of ease?

He said: Does he not find bread to eat, and have a wife in whom he finds repose and with whom he lies? I mentioned this to Abū ʿAbdillāh, and he said: He is right. He began to say, “To Allah we belong and to Him we return,” and said: We do eat our fill.
Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith said: I have not eaten my fill for fifty years. He also said: It is not fitting for a man today to eat his fill even of what is lawful,
because when he eats his fill of what is lawful, his self calls him to what is unlawful. So what of these filthy things?

From Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, who said: Whoever controls his stomach controls his religion, and whoever masters his hunger masters good character. Disobedience to Allah is far from the hungry and near to the full. Being full deadens the heart, and from it come exultation, frivolity and laughter.

Thābit al-Bunānī said: It has reached us that Iblīs appeared to Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both), and he saw things of every kind hanging on him. Yaḥyā said to him: Iblīs, what are these things I see hanging on you?
He said: These are the appetites with which I catch the children of Ādam. He said: Is there anything of mine among them?
He said: Sometimes you eat your fill, and we make you too heavy for prayer and remembrance. He said: Is there anything else? He said:
No. He said: I vow to Allah never again to fill my stomach with food. Iblīs said: And I vow to Allah never again to give sincere counsel to a Muslim.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: When the self is hungry and thirsty, the heart becomes pure and tender; when it is full and has drunk its fill, the heart becomes blind. He also said: The key to this world is being full, and the key to the Hereafter is hunger.

The root of all good in this world and the Hereafter is fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah gives this world to those He loves and those He does not love, but hunger He keeps in treasuries stored up with Him, and He gives it only to those He loves in particular.
To leave a morsel of my supper is dearer to me than to eat it and then stand [in prayer] from the beginning of the night to its end.
Al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā al-Khushanī said: Whoever wants his tears to flow freely and his heart to be tender, let him eat and drink in half his stomach. Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said:
I told Abū Sulaymān this, and he said: The hadith only says, “A third for food and a third for drink.” I see that these people have taken themselves to account and gained a sixth.
Muḥammad ibn al-Naḍr al-Ḥārithī said: Hunger spurs one to righteousness just as a full belly spurs one to insolence.
From al-Shāfiʿī, who said: I have not eaten my fill for sixteen years, except once, and that I threw up;
for being full weighs the body down, takes away sharpness of mind, brings on sleep and weakens a person for worship.
The Prophet ﷺ encouraged eating little in the hadith of al-Miqdām, saying: “A few mouthfuls are enough for the son of Ādam to keep his back upright.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs it is reported from him ﷺ that he said:

“The believer eats in one intestine, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.” What is meant is that the believer eats with the manners of the Sharīʿah, and so eats in one intestine, while the disbeliever eats as appetite, greed and voracity dictate, and so eats in seven intestines.

Besides eating little and making do with part of the food, he ﷺ encouraged giving the rest of it to others, saying: “The food of one is enough for two, the food of two is enough for three, and the food of three is enough for four.”

The best way for the believer to eat, then, is to eat in a third of his stomach, drink in a third and leave a third for breath, as the Prophet ﷺ mentioned in the hadith of al-Miqdām; for drinking much brings on sleep and spoils the food.
Sufyān said: Eat what you like, but do not drink; if you do not drink, sleep will not come to you.

One of the Salaf said: There were young men among the Children of Israel who devoted themselves to worship. When it was time for them to break their fast, someone would stand over them and say: Do not eat much, or you will drink much, then sleep much, then lose much.

The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions often went hungry and ate little of the foods people crave. Even if that was because food was not to be had, Allah chooses for His Messenger only the most perfect and best of states.
That is why Ibn ʿUmar imitated them in this, though he was able to obtain food, as his father had done before him.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿĀʾishah, who said: From the time he came to Madīnah until he was taken, the family of Muḥammad ﷺ never ate their fill of wheat bread for three nights in a row.
In Muslim's version she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never ate his fill of barley bread two days in succession until he was taken.
Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never ate his fill of food for three days until he was taken.
Also from him, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left this world without having eaten his fill of barley bread.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿUmar: He gave a sermon and mentioned the worldly gains that people had acquired, and said: I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spend the whole day doubled over [with hunger], unable to find even poor dates (daqal) to fill his stomach.
Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I have been harmed for the sake of Allah when no one else was being harmed,
and I have been made to fear for the sake of Allah when no one else was made to fear. Three days and nights have passed over me when I had no food except what Bilāl's armpit could hide.”
Ibn Mājah recorded with his chain from Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to us, and we stayed three nights unable — or: he was unable — to find any food.

Also with his chain, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: Hot food was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he ate. When he had finished, he said: “Praise be to Allah! No hot food has entered my stomach since such-and-such a time.”

Allah and His Messenger have censured those who follow their appetites. The Exalted said: “Then there came after them successors who neglected the prayer and followed their appetites; they will meet perdition — except those who repent” [Maryam 19:59–60].

It is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best generation is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them. Then will come people who bear witness without being asked to bear witness, who make vows and do not fulfil them, and among whom fatness appears.”
In the Musnad: The Prophet ﷺ saw a fat man and began pointing with his hand at his belly, saying: “If this were somewhere other than here, it would be better for you.”
In the Musnad, from Abū Barzah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “What I fear most for you is the appetites of error in your stomachs and your private parts, and the whims that lead astray.”

In the Musnad of al-Bazzār and elsewhere, from Fāṭimah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The worst of my nation are those who are nourished on luxury, who eat every kind of food, wear every kind of clothing and speak with affected eloquence.”

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man belched in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: “Keep your belching away from us, for those who eat their fill most in this world will be hungry longest on the Day of Resurrection.”
Ibn Mājah also recorded something similar from the hadith of Salmān,
and al-Ḥākim recorded it from the hadith of Abū Juḥayfah; all their chains are open to criticism.
Yaḥyā ibn Mandah narrated in his book Manāqib al-Imām Aḥmad (“The Virtues of Imam Aḥmad”), with a chain of his own, that Imam Aḥmad was asked about the words of the Prophet ﷺ:
“A third for food, a third for drink and a third for breath.” He said: The third for food is sustenance; the third for drink is strength; and the third for breath is the spirit. And Allah knows best.
